people.narrative_profile: Political partner whom Elias meets on the 1849–50 princely tour. His humiliating experience of American racial prejudice undercuts faith in U.S. protection. On taking the throne in 1854, he negotiates limits on the California alliance and appoints his sister Victoria Kamāmalu Kuhina Nui in January 1855. He authorizes Hawaiian consent through the kingdom's institutions and supports limits on emergency government. His death in November 1863 leaves Lot to inherit an unequal political alliance. **Voice:** Deliberation under pressure, royal dignity and the experience of a man who has compared empires from within.

Elias's closest Hawaiian royal friend, attached to riding, the outdoors and the right of rulers to act decisively. The friendship begins before treaties. Lot succeeds in 1863, seeks stronger Hawaiian royal authority and retains the Kuhina Nui, judging abolition politically contentious. He bargains with Victoria as a continuing co-executive and supports the 1865 enabling settlement in exchange for guarantees protecting kingship, her office, local institutions and agreed revenues. His confidence in decisive government coexists with resistance to confederal encroachment; the guarantees' wording remains open. He does not live to witness the 1874 lease and later illegal ordinances, dying in December 1872 with his sister Victoria designated heir under Article 22 of his 1864 constitution. **Voice:** Direct and stubborn, neither a Hawaiian Elias-clone nor an arbitrary obstacle.

Monarch whose government considers U.S. annexation in the 1854 crisis. Elias's offer of protection without absorption helps preserve Hawaiian independence at the time. His death in December 1854 changes the diplomatic situation.

Alexander’s wife from June 1856 and Anglican widow after 1863. She leads the London-oriented loyalists and becomes their counter-queen after the 1874 lease and ordinances, until her death in 1885. In 1883 she builds outside the leased Puʻuloa ground and plants banyans and two thousand coconuts at the fleet’s gate. Queen’s Hospital is her foundation; Noe nurses there in 1881 and gains loyalist patrons. After Emma’s death loyalists look to Albert Kūnuiākea. **Voice/POV:** Royal dignity, household networks, Anglican ties and a political alternative to Victoria’s bargain. She is not elected queen in this timeline.

CR-027 identifies the former fictional Kaiulani with historical Victoria. This entry is retained solely as provenance and redirects to CT-KAIULANI, the active canonical identity and holder of all existing legacy mappings. It does not represent a second woman.

Victoria’s childhood betrothed; her brothers block the match for rank, estates and dynastic reasons, and in 1857 she chooses Elias over both him and Kalākaua. He leads opposition to Victoria after her accession in December 1872. He never reigns in this timeline and dies on 3 February 1874. His followers’ rising in the Queen’s name follows; she refuses it. His supporters have independent fears of confederal rule, rather than serving merely as a rejected suitor’s faction.

Foreign Minister associated with the Hawaiian negotiations. With Victoria he works out institutional state assent, member representation and emergency limits in the 1856 Articles. He supports the Hawaiian coalition restraining escalation at Washoe in 1860. His professional diplomatic caution can recognize the danger of executive concentration even when practical interests favor stronger common institutions; his exact role in the enabling settlement remains open.

Historical person born in 1836, the suitor Victoria refuses in 1857. He becomes her minister of the image and envoy, never controller of the purse. He revives hula, prints genealogical chants and retells legends, including the Iron Knife as a prehistory for Japanese partnership. Suspected of a hand in the 1873 mutiny, he is made answerable for the surviving Guard; Judd later serves him. He brings nobles to the lawful Puʻuloa lease. In 1881 he tours the world for the Queen with Judd, proposes an Oceanian union and the Kaʻiulani–Komatsu match to Meiji, and is declined. Hoʻoulu Lāhui stands over the mortality figures. His book’s account of Kekuaokalani is published under the fourth Kaʻahumanu’s patronage. He dies in San Francisco in 1891; the Five’s press seat inherits his image work. **Voice:** A maker of genealogical legitimacy and foreign prestige, whose Victorianized retellings remain his versions. Not Victoria’s younger nephew and not the unresolved later officers called Kalākaua.

**APPROVED — CR-029:** Carries a Polynesian compact to Malietoa Laupepa in 1886–1887 after Hawaii's 1878 Pago Pago treaty on the Confederation's behalf. Germany deports Malietoa while Pacifica is burying Elias, and no intervention follows. The failure belongs to his diplomatic career and to the succession's limits, rather than implying he reigned over Hawaii.

Engineer and aide linked to the founder's communications, campaigns and large projects. His role may become a continuing eyewitness to organizational failures, but his timeline must be checked before using him across decades.

---

**Status:** Author-approved characterization direction; Civil War meetings, concessions and campaign chronology remain **[OPEN]**. Historical Jefferson Davis in an alternate timeline; fictional actions and assigned motives are not historical testimony.

His single six-year presidency ends in February 1868, succeeded by Joseph E. Johnston after the 1867 election. The 1865 peace preserves the government he defended while leaving it increasingly dependent on Pacifica; it does not give him a postwar presidency without limit.

Davis seeks to preserve a government with legitimate political authority, rather than a Southern administration surviving at Thorne's pleasure. His dominant commitments are sovereignty, inherited republican obligation and public responsibility. He can understand Pacifica's superior force while disputing that force creates a right to govern. His position includes the slaveholding order in which he has a planter's stake; the consent he invokes does not extend equally to the people that order enslaves.

His conflict with Benjamin concerns the permissible price of independence. Immediate relief may preserve soldiers and households while permanently surrendering customs, ports or jurisdiction. Ericsson has an established engineering career and American attachments before California's purchasing network approaches him. Disappointment with his large caloric ship and the unbuilt 1854 armored-warship proposal create an opening for Pacifican patronage. Marcus's eastern procurement relationships arrange a commercial assignment around 1855, initially concerned with pumps, stationary machinery and screw propulsion. Elias offers a paid visit, experimental facilities associated with an operating foundry, commercial rights and funded trials. Ericsson retains relationships with eastern partners including Delamater; their exact contracts and response to the later war remain open.

The assignment becomes a sustained commitment during the working 1856–1858 period. Thorne earns his confidence through serious technical questions, respect for agreed terms and support through failure. Their proposed first meeting involves disagreement over caloric engines and measurable performance; its dialogue and precise circumstances are not fixed. Commercial caloric applications, reliable steam propulsion and experimental armored defense remain distinct undertakings. He helps develop machinery, testing practice and skilled teams, then the experimental turret programme around 1859–1860. Manufacturing, imported armor and guns, finance and crews remain essential to his achievements.

Logan Turner becomes a gifted junior within this community after adolescent migration from Kentucky. Donahue's workshops are a proposed route into the programme. Ericsson teaches precision, compact machinery and whole-vessel integration. Logan presses questions about fuel, wear, maintenance and imperfect operators. Their relationship contains mutual respect and professional friction, not automatic agreement between two universal geniuses. Logan takes these lessons east in 1861 before the Columbia ironclad fights; Ericsson does not accompany the Confederate mission.

War forces Ericsson to choose among genuine commitments. He remains in Pacifica and supports its naval defense while resisting the assumption that all his work is automatically available to the Confederacy. American ties make this a difficult decision; legal nationality, contractual limits and specific acts of refusal remain open. His designs and team contribute to an armored battery assembled on the lower Columbia and used against a federal recovery attempt in 1862. Its success depends on industrial partners, supporting vessels, pilots and Marcus's forces. Ericsson is not its naval commander or an infallible battlefield rescuer. His absence from the United States removes the historical Monitor intervention at Hampton Roads and changes later armored production, while rival Union designers and the western river fleet retain agency.

Neither his surname nor his birthplace establishes mixed ancestry; parentage beyond the approved family description remains open.

His loyalties, choices and consequences require scenes, not a predetermined betrayal.

The Inspectorate helps finance the 1906 Chinese technical university, whose graduates become China's own officials and nationalists. In 1928–1929 the Inspectorate returns, the school becomes a joint Sino-Pacifican foundation and the revenue administration becomes a Concord affair with a Japanese deputy, both officers commissioned by China. His dilemma includes financing the elite that will demand an end to foreign administration; he is not automatically the Formosan Director-General.

These detailed articles remain PROPOSED in the supplied treaty passage. They strengthen Chinese bargaining power without making the Pacifican Inspectorate Chinese sovereignty or making Fong the unprovided signer of Harbin.

people.display_name: Kiyoshi’s son, the next Kuroda generation
people.narrative_profile:

He is distinct from Kiyoshi’s resolved Fleet-General alias and from Julian’s son Kahekili. **Open:** Name, age, mother, career and personal motives. CR-021’s 1932 renewal ends the naval party’s reserved-squadron arrangement as overseas command becomes common; the Navy ministry is then part of the bargain.


He keeps the Japanese units loyal in 1932 with the lesson of his father’s 1907 bid: a fleet cannot make a sovereign. Kiyoshi’s branch is distinct from the main house held by Kiyonaka.

**CR-045 (31 October 2026):** APPROVED: from 1920 he reads Maria Grishina-Almazova's reports from her Tokyo salon for the Navy General Staff; in May 1932 her warning tells him which ships and which day. PROPOSED: his posting in the intelligence division in the 1920s before the western squadron. **CR-046:** he never learns that British gold paid the Chekists on Kronstadt in his father's last weeks.

**Status:** Historical person; alternate partnership and detailed incidents PROPOSED under CR-018 D4 and CR-019. Raises Japanese war loans in San Francisco in 1904–1905 and becomes Tokyo’s financial partner for Thalassia. In the 1927 crisis he and Chiyo negotiate the Concord; in 1931 he receives Julian’s threat through her. His actual California experience is a source-supplied historical anchor, not independent proof of these events. **Open:** Agreements, personal exchanges and changed political fate. CR-020 B14 makes San Francisco’s provision of Japan’s 1927 crisis borrowing decisive; the rescue scales with Japan’s richer economy. Amounts and debt ratios remain MODEL estimates. Gold parity later aggravates rural distress until the adjustable 1932 order. CR-021 approves his three-week moratorium in April 1927 as the time the bargain needs. **CR-024–CR-025, current model:** The three-week moratorium separates Japanese recapitalization and secured yen liquidity from an external payments shortage. Japan uses its own capital and Bank of Japan money; Julian's public/private San Francisco credit supplies foreign exchange. The supplied model estimates approximately $400m replacement capital, $295m BOJ liquidity and $497m foreign drawing within $600m committed. These are MODEL estimates, not Takahashi's historical accounts, and do not establish a new common-minister appointment for him.

people.display_name: Herbert Hoover, Pacifican relief and moratorium official
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Pacifican identity, the 1927 Gulf flood relief and June 1931 war-debt moratorium settled by CR-020 B5–B6. Exact relief-to-treasury appointments and chronology remain qualified under OPEN-019-04. CR-051 (APPROVED) supersedes the earlier proposed Belgian relief: a belligerent Pacifica does not feed occupied Belgium; that work is the neutral Union's.

Hoover's administrative competence belongs to a different sovereign state. During the Mississippi flood the Gulf prosecutes planters who hold Black refugees in levee camps, and its statistics remain honest. In the Depression his moratorium on Pacifica's war-debt claims helps limit forced selling; the order restructures rather than calls its debts. Dawes is the Union president and bears responsibility for Union tariff and farm policy. **Open:** Exact titles, appointment instruments, personal exchanges and the remaining earlier career details.

**APPROVED — CR-051:** Born in Iowa in 1874 and raised in Oregon from 1885, he takes his geology degree at Carquinez in 1895, works as a mining engineer in Australia and China (in the siege of Tientsin in 1900 he helps build the barricades and organises food and water) and as a mining financier in London in 1902–1914. In the war he is Pacifica's food administrator, and in 1918–1919 he holds the food lever under Julian's timing. At The Hague in 1919 he decides where Pacifican food and credit go, and secures the uranium side of the Joachimsthal and Shinkolobwe concessions without asking why. In 1920 the Works' director and the keys admit him to the inner circle as head of the ore office (Fergana, the world survey, the stockpile); Lou Henry Hoover, examined in geology, works with him on the survey. In 1925 he leaves the ore office for public office, still under his bond, an inner-circle man who must answer the Senate about the Works' purchases without a false word. In 1926 he backs Szilárd's five years against the Chief's twenty: ore turns up wherever someone looks. **Open:** whether so famous a figure suits the ore office; scenes. *(Irony: historically he campaigned against foreign raw-material cartels; here he builds the largest.)*

**Status:** Union president 1901–1909 and refused mediator in 1905 approved by CR-019; the 1903 emulation and containment response approved by CR-020 B13/E21.

Pacifica Steel's successful 1901 Carnegie purchase gives Roosevelt a public cause. He presents the loss of firms, patents and skilled people as a national problem, while Wall Street's role in the foreign sale feeds resentment. From 1903 he funds technical institutions and laboratories, supports a central bank and intact industrial champions, and combines talent-retention measures with patent licensing and tariffs against Pacifican firms. Taft and Wilson continue the programme as it reaches full force by 1910. Pacifica answers by recruiting skilled Asians.

Caribbean pressure, Japanese courtship, the Cape Horn fleet voyage, Bull Moose split and attacks on wartime neutrality retain their earlier proposal status. **Open:** Particular speeches, legislative instruments, private motives and scenes. The Union is an adaptive rival with substantial remaining power, rather than a passive source of Pacifican talent.

**Status:** Union president 1909–1913 under CR-019 A9. CR-020 B13 settles his continuation of Roosevelt's programme to emulate Pacifica at home and contain it abroad, fully in force by 1910. Exact legislation, private motives and other alternate incidents remain unspecified.

**Status:** Union president 1913–1921; Union neutrality approved. The proposed course connects his election to Roosevelt’s split and makes him refuse Germany’s 1917 recovery offer. He supplies neither a Union expeditionary army nor the European peace’s controlling leverage. CR-020 B13 also settles his continuation of the Union’s emulation and containment programme. Neutrality and the preference for financial investment help explain why the Union does not simply outbuild the Pacific alliance.
**Status:** Union president from 1921 until Coolidge succeeds in 1923, within CR-019 A9’s approved sequence. Historical baseline; alternate private and policy detail unassigned.

**Status:** Union president 1923–1929 in the approved sequence. The proposed European lending boom belongs to his period. Historical baseline; no additional incident inferred. Under CR-020, European lending competes with naval spending until the 1927 Concord prompts three additional Union capital ships; the crash halts further construction. Ship counts remain MODEL estimates.

**Status:** Union president 1929–1933 approved by CR-019 A9. Architect of the Union’s German loans who presides over their collapse on the proposed course. His term includes the conditional second gold rescue and Thalassia settlement. CR-020 gives his Union responsibility for its own tariff and farm choices. The Union’s press resents the 1932 nominal-income crossing, while the country retains larger real output and its emulation and containment strategy. CR-021 revision 9 expressly assigns him acceptance of the gold rescue and negotiation of association as the choice against bank collapse; Young’s campaign and later endorsement follow, without moving the presidential dates. APPROVED — CR-043 P4: at The Hague in 1919 he sits in Bryan's delegation for the Union's lenders, the beginning of his public life as their custodian.

**Status:** Elected Union president in November 1932, approved by CR-019 A9; takes office in 1933. Electrical industrialist and finance specialist whose campaign accepts the Thalassia order and reconstruction through cooperation. Franklin Roosevelt supports him; unprovided policy and cabinet details remain qualified. CR-021 revision 9 settles the distinction: Dawes accepts the rescue and negotiates association; Young campaigns for acceptance of the settlement and endorses it as president-elect after November 1932. Hoover is its Pacifican face; Young takes office in 1933.

**Status:** Cooperation with Young and defeat of the alternative 1932 presidential outcome approved. Naval service under Wilson and New York governorship follow the proposed career. Secretary of the Navy under Young is a recommendation under OPEN-019-12, not an appointed office in 1932.

**Status:** Historical person redirected to Pacifica by CR-020 B9/E11. Arrives in San Francisco in 1884 and works within the electrical programme, including the institute established in 1886. Polyphase AC patents and the national standard connect his research with the champions. The Polytechnic offers laboratories and citizenship for chairs without national or religious tests. **Open:** Exact appointment, citizenship instrument, contracts, collaborators, private motives and changed later life. His alternate inventions and relationships must develop through work rather than historical name recognition alone.


**APPROVED — CR-027:** One of the Five in 1887, holding the power seat. **APPROVED — CR-052:** Harris J. Ryan succeeds him in 1924 (CR-027's proposed Steinmetz succession is retired).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** His works supply the counter's steady high voltage (1885–1887), build valve amplifiers with the Light and Matter Works by about 1895, and power Hillebrand's electric furnaces for uranium metal and graphite.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** Irving Langmuir comes to his electrical institute in 1903 and becomes his student. Past sixty, Tesla is the magnet halls' patron, showman and source of power; his grand visions against Langmuir's patient measurements are the halls' quarrel. He leaves the power seat at sixty-eight in 1924; Harris J. Ryan succeeds him (CR-052).

**APPROVED — CR-051:** Out of the Five from 1924 but still the halls' patron, he presses in 1926–1927 with Szilárd to shorten the Columbia's cooling times, and the Chief refuses.

**Status:** Historical person recruited to a Polytechnic chair in 1889 under CR-020 B9/E11. AC theory and turbo-generator work strengthen the electrical programme. **Open:** Appointment terms, collaborators, private life and specific scenes; source-supplied technical roles do not make every historical invention automatically Pacifican.


**Superseded — CR-052 CT9:** CR-027's proposed succession to the Five's power seat is retired: Steinmetz dies in October 1923, a year before Tesla's retirement, and Harris J. Ryan takes the seat in 1924. His 1889 arrival remains independently approved. CR-050 had him build the magnet halls' electrical supply; Harris J. Ryan builds it (CR-052). His works' regulating gear remains among the halls' bottlenecks after 1927 (CR-051).

**Status:** Historical person redirected to Polytechnic chemistry in 1889 under CR-020 B9/E11. Photographic paper and the later plastics programme connect the university to film and chemicals; Bakelite in 1907 is the approved programme's named milestone. **Open:** Appointment, patent agreements, collaborators, private motives and changed later career.


**PROPOSED — CR-027:** A later successor among the Five as the realm’s needs change; precise tenure and portfolio are not settled.

**Status:** Historical person in an approved alternate Gulf role under CR-020 B5. He attacks the examination franchise as an assault on the common white voter and loses. His constituency has its own political demands within the sovereign Gulf Republic; Pacifica's admission standards threaten planter power and local political machines. **Open:** Campaign date, office held, personal alliances and scene-level outcome. His opposition does not imply that the Gulf is admitted by 1932.

**Status:** Historical person with approved alternate relationship and Concord choices under CR-021 F/E. Crown Prince in 1921, Regent from November 1921, Emperor from 25 December 1926. Private thoughts in the novel are fictional characterization.

His absent, ill father and education under elders leave him studying a founder's model, as Julian studies Elias. On the 1921 tour home from Europe he travels by the Atlantic and Pacifica's canal to Thalassia. Weeks with Julian offer informal conversation in Japanese without an interpreter. He dives Kāneʻohe's reef once as crown prince; after becoming Regent he does not return to Pacifica. The Moku o Loʻe station exchanges specimens with his laboratory and its zoologists work with him at Hayama.

Julian's arrival with fleet relief and reconstruction credit after the 1923 earthquake builds gratitude. After the 1924 marriage Nagako and Chiyo become confidantes. Marine biology offers intimacy outside protocol; Julian's personal command also shows Hirohito what a more direct ruler might be. Their trust does not include the Altai secret, which Julian withholds.

In 1927 he follows Saionji's counsel and accepts the Concord on Julian's Japanese word: no lender offers equivalent rescue, and a fallen cabinet could expose the throne to the army. Privy Council conditions and Diet funding protect Japan's legal position. He retains crown, domestic institutions and the right to refuse renewal. At the annual Hayama Council from 1928 he hosts as Emperor while Julian convenes and presides; his brother Prince Chichibu represents him at Thalassia, with a Pacifican education, honors and outdoorsman reputation that make the alignment personal. In May 1932 he opposes officers claiming to restore his direct rule, choosing the constitutional arrangement and his friend. The crowns agree renewal at Hayama; ministers sign and exchange instruments at Thalassia. He does not travel there, and renewal lasts only to 1937.

**Desire:** Preserve the throne and Japan's freedom within a viable constitutional order. **Contradiction:** Protecting the crown through restraint and foreign trust exposes him to loyalists invoking his own authority against him. **Voice/POV:** Cautious court language loosening around specimens and shared work; knowledge of concealed Pacifican crimes must not be invented. **Open:** Specific private exchanges, scientific scenes and unprovided domestic details; the Council never requires him to sail to Thalassia.

**CR-029–CR-031 limits:** Julian's Realm, Hawaiian and Philippine crowns form one Concord party opposite Japan's crown; their internal council is not another Japanese vote. The proposed Kamchatka Resident and Company belong to Japan's protected northern sphere, while Siberian commercial passage and Chinese railway rights constrain the settlement. CR-031-R1 places Company employment within Japan’s professional construction system; these institutional arrangements assign Hirohito neither personal management of its contractors nor knowledge of the Altai crime.

people.display_name: Prince Chichibu, resident prince and Pacifican outdoorsman
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in an approved alternate Pacifican career, expressly selected by the author on 20 October 2026 (CR-021 revision 9). Hirohito’s brother and the Emperor’s resident representative at Thalassia in the Concord era.

In 1925–1926 he studies at the Polytechnic of Carquinez rather than taking the Oxford route. Pacifican officers, engineers, field excursions and companions give him connections before the Concord makes him resident prince. His education is part of Japan’s turn toward Pacifica as a source of prestige, not a British chapter followed by an administrative posting overseas.

He develops his outdoorsman reputation in the Sierra and Hawaiian uplands, traveling with Pacifican companions and local guides. The Crown honors him, and press and newsreels make that life familiar. Recognition and the landscapes he knows belong to the realm, while his Japanese identity and rank remain his own. Specific decorations, named climbs and companions are unprovided; no medal, military rank or summit record is invented.

At Thalassia he represents Hirohito between the annual Hayama Councils and sits beside the throne at the opening of the Senate’s Season. He is neither a common minister nor an independent commander. In 1932 ministers sign and exchange the renewal instruments in Thalassia after the crowns agree them at Hayama; his presence does not substitute for his brother’s constitutional consent. He does not know the Altai secret.

His enjoyment of the outdoors is real, even when court publicity turns it into evidence for the Concord. Restoration officers can attack a prince of their own house who has made friendships and a public life in the realm they call a foreign bakufu. He wants competence and freedom in the field while bearing a representative’s rank and obligations at court.

**Desire:** Earn recognition through useful experience and field competence while representing Japan with dignity. **Contradiction:** A freely chosen Pacifican life becomes a political image others want to control. **Voice/POV:** Attentive to routes, weather, pace, companions and local knowledge; formality returns when he represents his brother. Guides and companions have agency beyond serving a prince’s reputation. **Open:** Particular decorations, climbs, companions, private exchanges and unprovided appointment dates; the resident identity, Pacifican orientation and career direction are settled.

**Status:** approved_alternate_role (CR-027).

Victoria’s half-sister, a major landholder and governor of Hawaiʻi island, speaks no English and keeps the old ways. Victoria appoints her Kuhina Nui on accession in 1872. She countersigns the lawful Puʻuloa lease, then refuses the appointed Territorial Council and resigns; the office remains vacant. Victoria retains her own estate, so Ruth’s eventual holdings are smaller than in history. Exact instrument dates remain PROPOSED under CR-027 A13.

**Status:** approved_alternate_role (CR-027).

After Emma dies in 1885, Hawaiian loyalists look to her cousin and heir Albert, widely understood to be Kamehameha III’s unacknowledged natural son. He has squandered his inheritance. He represents a continuing loyalist alternative to Victoria’s bargain; no reign or successful revolt is supplied.

**Status:** approved_alternate_role (CR-027).

A missionary’s son and Victoria’s Royal School schoolmate, adjutant general during the September 1873 Guard mutiny. Victoria dismisses him along with Jajczay on the first day. Sacrificed by his own party’s Queen, he attaches himself to Kalākaua and accompanies the 1881 world tour as chamberlain.

**Status:** approved_alternate_role (CR-027).

Hungarian veteran of the hussars who escorted Maximilian to Mexico, hired by Lot to drill a Guard independent of Monterey’s academy. His imprisonment of four soldiers for deserting the treasury post triggers the September 1873 mutiny. Victoria dismisses him; he leaves the islands and dies in Costa Rica in 1874. The first-day resolution and retained Guard are alternate history.

**Status:** approved_alternate_role (CR-027).

people.display_name: Princess Kaʻiulani of the Cleghorn household
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** approved_minor_historical_identity (CR-027); a principal of the 1919 peace from CR-043 (31 October 2026).

The historical princess born in 1875, a minor figure in the Cleghorn household and Kalākaua’s niece. In his 1881 mission he proposes her marriage to Prince Komatsu as part of an Oceanian union; Meiji declines. Distinct from Victoria Kamāmalu (CT-KAIULANI), born in 1838. The ʻokina distinguishes her name in CR-027.

APPROVED — CR-043 P1: she lives. Schooled in England from 1889. Graves' disease (exophthalmic goitre) is diagnosed in 1896, and in 1897 Theodor Kocher at Bern ties off the gland's arteries and then removes part of it, leaving her enough. Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars, which decrees the Red Terror on 5 September 1918; author of the Penza telegram of 11 August 1918. Leaves Moscow before it falls in March 1920 by the northern road toward Vyatka, and is taken at the Kotelnich bridge by the Pacifican armoured train *Pele* under Major George S. Patton (CT-GEORGE-PATTON) and Russian cavalry on 22 April 1920, his fiftieth birthday (CR-041, CR-044). Tried with Trotsky before a Russian court in Moscow for state crimes of which he is guilty, charged with the Romanov murder, and executed in late 1920. His Kamchatka concession to a Los Angeles engineer, signed in his government's last winter, is repudiated at Harbin.

Orders the Czechoslovak Legion disarmed on 25 May 1918, the trigger of the coalition's move; brings the canal destroyers to the Volga and loses before Kazan in September 1918; orders the arrest of the families of defecting officers on 30 September 1918. On 25 February 1920 he takes his command train south to hold the Oka at Serpukhov, is cut off by Wrangel's cavalry at Lopasnya, fights the Volunteer train *Ofitser* across the river, and surrenders at first light on 27 February after a night siege. From the dock he names Lenin for the Romanov decision, and it does not save him; executed in late 1920.

**Character use:** His orders are historical documents; his capture is the Russian army's action, with no Pacifican hand in it.

Directed the recapture of Krasnaya Gorka from the sea in June 1919 and told Lenin he deplored the naval science that called it impossible (*hist.*). When Moscow falls in March 1920 he slips away south and is next heard of in Tiflis; Georgia's Menshevik government will not hand a Georgian to a Russian court. His road south is OPEN. He is never tried. Whether and when he resurfaces is OPEN. The Kronstadt role of the original K1 passes to Dzerzhinsky (CT-FELIX-DZERZHINSKY).

Thalassia hesitates; a British secret-service watcher on the envoy's door recognises Kamo; in the autumn of 1921 Stalin is shot in Tiflis by Georgians with old reasons of their own, London having arranged the occasion. He vetoes the partition of Austria-Hungary, which would ruin the Union's Vienna loans, and signs the Treaty of The Hague on 28 June 1919 for the mediating Union; the Senate then refuses the naval limits and the court. An old railway surveyor who comes out to Russia with the Pacifican railway mission in 1916 and stays through the revolutions. Taken hostage in Petrograd in September 1918 and spared when eleven of the advisers are shot, he is moved to Kronstadt in 1920 and is the first of the Pacifican advisers brought up alive from the *Petropavlovsk*'s hostage deck after Kiyoshi's cut. Born in 1884 at Hilo, grandson of one of the 1868 emigrants from Japan to Hawaiʻi (the *Gannenmono*, *hist.*), of a Satsuma family. A traffic engineer of the Carquinez Polytechnic's railway school, a man who counts wagons. He comes to Russia with the 1916 railway mission. He is one of the eleven advisers shot in the first week of September 1918, the week Cromie dies.

**Character use:** The reader meets him once before he dies; keep him exact, unheroic and professional.

Born at San Gabriel, California, in 1885 (*hist.*), so a Pacifican by birth in this history. Grandson of a Confederate colonel killed at Third Winchester and of Benjamin Davis Wilson, the Los Angeles rancher and mayor of 1851 (*hist.*). An Olympic pentathlete in 1912 and designer of the 1913 cavalry sabre (*hist.*). **APPROVED — CR-058:** Funston's aide in the ninety-day expedition into Chihuahua of 1916. On 14 May 1916 at the San Miguelito ranch near Rubio, with three Pacifican-built touring cars, about ten soldiers and civilian guides and drivers, he kills Julio Cárdenas, commander of Villa's Dorados, and two other men and straps the bodies to the bonnets: the first motorised raid in his service's history (*hist.*: under Pershing). The lesson of speed, engines and nerve takes him to the armoured trains. A cavalry major seconded to the railway brigade's armoured trains, he commands *Pele* at the Kotelnich bridge with two squadrons of Russian cavalry and takes Lenin on 22 April 1920. PROPOSED: he declines to come aboard Lenin's train, the theatrical correctness of a man who thinks war should have manners; a natural player for the 1920s.

**Character use:** Flamboyant, superstitious, a horseman and a reader of military history; keep the historical man's temperament and give his Pacifican career its own facts as they are decided.

Major-General, head of the British military mission in Siberia (*hist.*). French general, appointed to command the Allied and Czechoslovak forces in Siberia; Omsk gave a city banquet in his honour on the evening of 17 November 1918 while he was still on his way, and he reached the city only in December (*hist.*, **VERIFY** the date). Ivan Adrianovich Mikhailov, born in a convict prison, the son of a revolutionary; a political economist from Petrograd and Siberia's finance minister at twenty-six, whom his enemies call Vanka-Kain (*hist.*). In August 1918 he tries and fails to bring the Kazan gold under his ministry's seal against the Reserve Bank's escrow. In September he decides Volkov's arrests with him and is saved from the Czech search by Pacifican orders. On the evening of 17 November 1918 he sells the coup to the paymaster Kashevarov, with his copy of the British mission's promise of credit, and is paid and held by Pacifica afterwards; Julian lets the coup begin so that it fails in public, and Mikhailov is dismissed, not given his ministry. At Harbin he heads the Chinese Eastern Railway's economic bureau (*hist.*), London's man on the surface and Pacifica's underneath, and keeps a ledger of his own; his reports are the first map of the Manchurian officers. Maria Grishina-Almazova refuses him in the winter of 1919–20. In 1921 he tells Julian to his face what the Tomsk vote has done to the 1918 promise. In June 1927 Kashevarov shows Churchill his copy of the Omsk promise, and in January 1928 Volkov, told by the British whose hand his papers were in, shoots him outside his house in Modyagou. (*Hist.:* he married Maria in 1921 and was shot in the USSR in 1946.)

**Character use:** The cleverest man in every room until he meets the one who holds the money. Charming, quick and unrepentant; never at the scene. His scenes: the railway car on 17 November; the refusal at Harbin; the hour with Julian in 1921.

**Status:** Invented; CR-045, APPROVED (31 October 2026; name OPEN); CR-046.

Pavel (Paul) Kashevarov, born about 1884 at Sitka, a Creole of Russian and Alutiiq descent, Orthodox and Russian-speaking, a Pacifican since 1867. PROPOSED: of the family of the navigator A. F. Kashevarov (**VERIFY**), who charted the Alaskan coast for the Russian-American Company and died a Russian general. The Reserve Bank's paymaster at Omsk from 1918, to whom the Kazan gold escrow at Chelyabinsk answers. He outplays Mikhailov over the gold, has the Czech search called off, buys the coup on 17 November and wires Julian, and reads Mikhailov's Harbin reports before London does. In April 1920, auditing the Moscow bank ledgers, he recognises the Petrograd account from Mikhailov's sheet (PROPOSED). Stalin's offer of 1921 reaches him. In June 1927, as head of the Reserve Bank's Russian department, he lays one sheet before Churchill, knowing it names Mikhailov; Julian is not told what it costs. His warning reaches Harbin later than it could have, and Mikhailov's ledger comes to him. He gives the whole Petrograd file to the Chronicler.

**Character use:** A ledger-keeper who sees Mikhailov's game because it is his own: a provincial, half an outsider, faster than his superiors. The one man on the Pacifican side who knows the full cost of the Omsk night. The storyline gives no verdict on him.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-045, APPROVED (31 October 2026). Sources: Petin, *Noveishaya istoriya Rossii* 9:2 (2019).

Maria Alexandrovna Grishina-Almazova, later Kashiwagi (1891–1976). A café singer in Khabarovsk before the war ("Wet Manka", *hist.*), wife of General Grishin-Almazov and hostess of Omsk's monarchist salon; Mikhailov's mistress from 1918. Mystical and given to fortune-tellers; her diary of 17 January 1919 records a prophecy that her husband will be taken far away against his will and killed, and that "another" will love her and give her everything (*hist.*); it holds, off the page. Her husband dies on the Caspian on 5 May 1919. In the winter of 1919–20 she refuses Mikhailov at Harbin, as she refused him historically at Irkutsk, and sails from Dalian to Japan. From 1920 she keeps a Russian salon in Tokyo and reports what she hears to the Navy General Staff; her reader is Kiyoshi's son. In 1921 she marries Commander Kashiwagi of the fleet faction; their son is baptised Georgy at Surugadai. Her reports become the second folder of Pacifica's British file. Kiyoshi's son sends her reports on to Thalassia. In May 1932 she gives the coup away for Georgy, for whom the Restoration's Japan would have no place, and her warning tells Kiyoshi's son which ships and which day; her husband is court-martialled, and that summer she takes their son to San Francisco, where she dies in 1976 (*hist.* place and year). She never learns that Mikhailov sold Volkov.

**Character use:** Tall, loud, generous, hard-drinking, clever; she wanted a child above all. Historically she lived "in the shadow of her husbands"; here she steps out of it once, does what Mikhailov did at Omsk for the opposite reason, and loses her marriage by it. At most two scenes: the refusal at Harbin and one evening in the Tokyo drawing room.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-045, APPROVED (31 October 2026). Dates and real post-1919 fate **VERIFY**.

Colonel V. I. Volkov, commanding the Omsk garrison and the Siberian Cossack officers (*hist.*). He makes the September 1918 arrests that end with Novoselov in the Zagorodnaya grove, and the arrests of the Directory's Socialist-Revolutionaries on 18 November; both times he swears on his honour that he had no accomplices (*hist.*). After the night he is tried, swears it again and believes it, and is cashiered. He lives in Harbin on almost nothing. In late 1927 the British let him read his own papers and tell him whose hand half of them are in, and in January 1928 he shoots Mikhailov in the street outside his house.

**Character use:** A loyal, limited officer who protected his patron twice and was sold by him once. No invented interiority beyond that.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-045, APPROVED (31 October 2026).

Alexei Nikolaevich Grishin-Almazov (1880–1919), first commander of the Siberian Army (*hist.*). He loses his ministry in September 1918 and goes south to Denikin. On 5 May 1919, crossing the Caspian toward Omsk with Denikin's letters, he is taken at sea and shoots himself (*hist.*); in this history the ship that takes the *Leila* is a Red armed steamer out of Astrakhan, since no Baltic destroyer reaches the Caspian.

**Character use:** Off the page; known through Maria and the news of his death.

**Status:** Invented; CR-045, APPROVED (31 October 2026); name and given name OPEN.

A Japanese destroyer officer who served beside the British at Malta in 1917–18 and under Kiyoshi at Kronstadt in 1920, and came home believing that Japanese sailors died there for a Pacifican's hostages. Kolchak becomes his friend. Of the fleet faction, and courted with his friends by the British naval attaché. He marries Maria Grishina-Almazova in 1921; their son is Georgy. By 1932 he is executive officer of one of the western squadron's Japanese-crewed carriers and one of the men who plan its part in the coup; he is court-martialled with the others. His sentence is OPEN.

**Character use:** A sincere man with a real grievance, not a villain; the prophecy's "another" whom Maria betrays.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-044 C4 (PROPOSED), CR-046 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Secretary of State for War 1919–21 and Chancellor of the Exchequer 1924–29 (*hist.*). He reads Knox's account of the Omsk night at the War Office in 1919 (CR-044). In June 1927, while London presses the Baku review, Kashevarov lays one sheet before him: the British mission's Omsk promise of credit, with a ledger reference pencilled in the margin. He recognises the account, does not ask where the sheet came from, and withdraws the review. PROPOSED: he never knew of the Copenhagen gold of 1920, which went through Lloyd George's government and the secret service, and cannot know what else Thalassia holds; the sheet also explains Victoria's conduct at the Romanov burial to him.

**Character use:** The British politician whose life's argument against Bolshevism Pacifica vindicated and whose country it humiliated. He is shown one sheet, never the file.

**APPROVED — CR-051:** In 1926 his Treasury, on Lindemann's advice, declines the separation factory Fowler's memo calls for. In the autumn of 1927 he sees the column of water in the newsreels; the memo is in his own files.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-046 (PROPOSED).

Head of British intelligence in Russia in 1916–17 and Secretary of State for Air in Baldwin's cabinet, 1924–29 (*hist.*). His station keeps the Petrograd account. Named by the Chronicler; not on the page in 1927. (*Hist.:* he wrote that Russian rightists tried to frame the British for Rasputin's murder.)

**Character use:** Off the page.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-046, APPROVED (31 October 2026).

Simon Ter-Petrosian, "Kamo" (1882–1922), who led the Tiflis bank robbery of 1907 and whose face was in Europe's newspapers after his arrest in Berlin that year (*hist.*). The only man Stalin trusts: in 1921 he carries Stalin's offer, with nothing on paper, overland by Kars to Pacifica's envoy at Ankara, where a British secret-service watcher on the envoy's door recognises him. PROPOSED: he dies in Tiflis on 14 July 1922 when a lorry runs down his bicycle (*hist.* date and manner); the Chronicler declines to say whether it was an accident.

**Character use:** No invented interiority.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-046 (PROPOSED).

Leo Steveni (1893–1972), with the British military mission in Petrograd from 1915 and Knox's liaison officer at the White Army's Omsk headquarters from November 1918 to November 1919 (*hist.*; King's College London, Liddell Hart Centre). PROPOSED: he initials the Omsk promise of credit, carrying the Petrograd account east.

**Character use:** Off the page.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R7, R11 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

At Atlanta University in the rump from 1897 to 1910 (*hist.*), where his Atlanta Studies take a grant from Pacifica's statistics bureau on condition that they follow the bureau's counting rules. He defends the grant against Montgomery and against Union theorists alike. His data charts for the Paris Exposition of 1900 (*hist.*) become the visual form the Office of Public Measures adopts. He crosses from the rump to found the Niagara Movement at Fort Erie in 1905, helps found the NAACP after Springfield and edits *The Crisis* in New York from 1910, whose first number carries the Parchman raid. He never moves to Pacifica. His feud with Garvey in the 1920s splits the movement between integration and separation.

**Character use:** Exact, proud, statistical and moral at once; the man who measures what others only feel. Keep him independent of Pacifica even while he takes its money.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R11 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Principal of Tuskegee in Alabama, inside the rump (*hist.* institution). He accommodates Montgomery, channels Union philanthropy into Tuskegee (Carnegie's 1903 gift among it, which the *Tribune* later counts as Pacifican money because Carnegie's income comes from a Pacifican company) and condemns the Parchman raid from Tuskegee in 1910. Dies in 1915 (*hist.*).

**Character use:** Patient, guarded, transactional; his realism is the rump's possible and its limit.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R11 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Born in Charleston in 1883, north at sixteen, at Howard from 1907, first Spingarn Medal 1915, doctorate at Chicago 1916 (*hist.*). Howard lives on a federal appropriation, so from 1911 he signs the Parchman Act's oath; no Union university or laboratory gives a Black zoologist a research post. After Chicago's riot of 1919 he takes a Carquinez research fellowship in 1920 attached to the survey of Kāneʻohe Bay for Keawe's Living Bay works. He is on the reef when the Crown Prince dives it in 1921, and from 1922 he directs the Crown's marine station on Moku o Loʻe, whose specimens and work at Hayama tie it to Hirohito's laboratory. Pacifican by examination. His cell-surface work is published from Moku o Loʻe.

**Character use:** Meticulous, wounded, proud of his craft; the arc's proof in one life that the Union's racism costs it talent and that Pacifica's door opens for the examined few.

**Status:** Invented; CR-048 R14 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Born about 1872 on a Coahoma County plantation in the Mississippi Delta, bound to his mother's master under the free-womb law; escapes to Memphis at fourteen and is a Union citizen within the year under the Freedom Act. Serves in the Union's Black cavalry in Cuba in 1898 and leaves a sergeant. On 16 October 1910, the anniversary of Harpers Ferry, he crosses from Memphis with about forty men, opens the camps at the Parchman prison farm and calls the Delta to rise. It does not. His men are killed or taken within four days, reprisals fall on uninvolved families, and Mississippi tries him at Indianola and hangs him in December 1910. Letters found on his men name the Northern professors who paid for the raid; the Parchman Act of 1911 follows.

**Character use:** Disciplined, scriptural, certain; a soldier who believes an example will be followed. Do not make him a cartoon of either martyr or fanatic.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R9 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

North Carolina's Black congressman for the Second District (*hist.* 1897–1901). In this history he enters the Union Congress with North Carolina's readmission and holds the seat until 1910, when the state's literacy test follows the end of the federal supervisors.

**Character use:** The fundamental conditions' last working voice in Congress.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R17 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Born in St. Ann's Bay, Jamaica, in 1887, a British subject (*hist.*). In Colón in 1910–1911 he sees West Indians paid well on Pacifica's canal and given no road to its citizenship. Founds the UNIA in 1914 and comes to Harlem in 1916; its divisions spread through the rump's Delta and Black Belt and absorb the generation that watched Parchman fail. *Look to the Pacific* becomes a slogan: the Pacific order is his proof of what non-white peoples can build. Meets the Klan's Edward Young Clarke in Atlanta in June 1922. Pacifica refuses his Black Star Line ships (its finances fail the published credit test) and his Honolulu lecture. Convicted in 1923, imprisoned at Leavenworth from 1925, deported to Jamaica in 1927 by the Union in concert with Britain; Thalassia refuses him too.

**Character use:** Magnetic, grandiose, wounded by contempt; a showman with a real argument. No Japanese contact.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history; CR-048 R17 (APPROVED, 31 October 2026).

Acting Imperial Wizard of the second Klan (*hist.*), refounded on Stone Mountain in the rump in 1915. Meets Garvey in Atlanta in June 1922; their meeting is the emblem of the emigration programme the rump's populists and Black nationalists share and the rump cannot pay for.

**Character use:** The Klan as a business and a sales pitch.

people.display_name: Charles Sanders Peirce, mathematician and logician
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in 1839, the son of Harvard's mathematician Benjamin Peirce, with an undistinguished examination record. PROPOSED: in the spring of 1856 Sylvester offers him a place at Carquinez, where achievement outranks rank, and he comes west at sixteen. APPROVED: the Calculation Office's youngest computer, he reads Boole and, after his seventeenth birthday, sails as the youngest fellow to Japan (1856–1857), where the Dutch-run naval school at Nagasaki tests him as hard as he tests it. In 1863 he sees Boole's algebra in the Office's telegraph relays and builds the relay arithmetic demonstrator; his circuits, designed on paper first, make the programmed calculator of 1876–1879 run. In 1867 a checking rule of his is shown by Kate Curran to have discarded real readings, and he acknowledges it in public. He fits the electroscope readings (1864), describes the transformation curves (1870), computes the scattering that proves the nucleus (1883), conjectures with Morley that mass and heat are one (1886) and works the neutron's recoils (1899). PROPOSED: a facial neuralgia from his late teens brings on his tempers; success makes him overconfident in elegant procedures; in 1888, nearly fifty, he loses the registers' work to Hollerith's cards. **Open:** the journey's dangers (O4), private life, death.

**Voice:** Quick, combative, delighted by an elegant proof and slow to forgive a dull one; generous to a worthy opponent.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** At sixty-nine he is the appointed respondent at the challenge evening of November 1908. He works out the energy of a split times the atoms in a block of uranium and asks whether the split releases neutrons; if it does, the prudent course is to assume a chain is possible and act before it is proved. The secret begins with his argument. In the late 1880s his fits to the scattering from foil after foil give each core a charge near half its atomic weight.

**APPROVED — CR-050-R1:** At the challenge evening of 1908 he gives the split its name, fission, borrowing Cohn's word for the way bacteria divide, his *Spaltpilze* of the 1870s; from the opening of 1927 the world uses it.

people.display_name: Kate Layne, later Curran and Brandegee, the laboratory's recorder
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in Tennessee in 1844 and raised in Folsom from the age of nine. PROPOSED: in 1860, at fifteen, she passes the Republic's examination, one of the first women to do so, and joins the recording staff of the Laboratory of Light, Electricity and Matter. APPROVED: in 1861, at sixteen, she follows up Niépce's published observation with plates and a gold-leaf electroscope and establishes that the activity belongs to uranium; Genth publishes under her name and his. She marries Hugh Curran in 1866 and keeps her post. In 1867 she shows that Peirce's checking rule has discarded real readings, some of them hers, and fights for her credit until the corrections column restores it in 1872. She runs the counting room of 1882–1883 whose observers count the flashes that prove the nucleus. She never studies medicine. **Open:** scenes, her later years and second marriage beyond the name.

**Voice:** Exact, dry and unrelenting about a reading; she keeps everything and forgets nothing owed.

links.relationship: rival and colleague; corrects his checking rule in 1867

people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** The historian (1815–1876) whose series on the old ways runs in the Honolulu press from 1866. He argues in print until his death over whether achievement and the masters of the crafts can carry *mana*, and how that sits with genealogy and the gods; the argument outlives him and frames Honolulu's later name for the Five, *nā Kahuna*. **Open:** scenes; no kinship with existing characters is invented.

**Voice:** Learned, polemical, rooted in genealogy and the chiefs' history.

people.display_name: William Francis Hillebrand, chemist, head of the Light and Matter Works
people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in Honolulu in 1853; Pacifican by birth. He goes from Oahu College to Carquinez and to Bunsen at Heidelberg and comes home in 1878. In 1879 he reports a gas from pitchblende as nitrogen; in 1881 he finds it is helium and prints the correction to his own claim, and remembers. He assays Talbert's Western Slope ore in 1881–1882, finds the isotopes' chemistry and the light lead of uranium ores (1884–1886), makes uranium metal and graphite in electric furnaces, and in 1908, trusting the chemistry, reads fission. The seat among the Five for the atomic estate is his (approved). PROPOSED: director of the Light and Matter Works at its charter in 1883, seated among the Five in 1887. He leaves the seat at sixty-eight in 1921. **Open:** his successor; family and scenes.

**Voice:** A careful analyst who distrusts his own first reading and trusts a chemistry he has checked twice.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** He withholds his own fission paper for verification in November 1908, stops licensing strong neutron sources abroad in December, tells Victoria and Soberanes, takes the chain result to Julian with Soberanes in 1909 and proposes the compromise of the sealed envelope: dated, witnessed, sealed and opened in due course. He sponsors Meitner into the inner circle in 1911. Langmuir succeeds him in 1921. He dies in Honolulu, where he was born, on 7 February 1925, after Julian has told him the year the seal will be opened; he keeps it to the end because his record is dated and safe, because the term guarantees the opening, because he is a native son among *nā Kahuna*, and because he believes Peirce's argument. In 1927 the corrections column gives him the split.

**APPROVED — CR-050-R1:** He lives to see the first device work on the Black Rock Desert in May 1924.

**APPROVED — CR-051:** From 1909 he throttles the neutron sources sold abroad instead of stopping them (supersedes the December 1908 stop), and keeps his group publishing true work around uranium so that no hole opens in the journals. In 1911, when the Nobel committee sounds out Carquinez, he withdraws his group from the transuranic prize pending verification, which is true; the corrections column records it in 1927. In 1912 he refuses Meitner's request to warn Rutherford privately that the satellite model is wrong. Until 1917 he leads the scientists' phase of the programme under the two keys; from 1917 he chairs the Council of the Seal as director, the Chief his equal under it.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in Gleiwitz in 1850 to a Jewish family; Helmholtz's student, who has named cathode rays. In 1876, at twenty-six, he takes an assistant's post under Genth with citizenship. With Michelson he announces the electron in 1879; he takes his doctorate in 1881 and becomes master of the Laboratory of Light, Electricity and Matter; in 1883 he proposes the compact nucleus, and his positive rays sort atoms by mass. He reads the neutral radiation of the 1890s as a hard ray, refuses Nagaoka the recoil measurement, and accepts the neutron in 1901. He keeps his chair and the credit for the nucleus, but the next generation's best students go to Ralston College. **Open:** scenes and private life.

**Voice:** Authoritative, exacting, slow to concede.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** He co-sponsors Meitner into the inner circle in 1911 and then, past sixty, attacks her conjecture of a rare light isotope at a challenge evening. It is his last stand, and he loses.

**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in 1865; newly graduated in physics at Tokyo, he is sent by the Japanese partnership to Carquinez in 1887. Refused the recoil measurement by Goldstein, he takes it to Ralston College, where Michelson's valve-amplified counter gives the neutron, announced in 1899. He knows the work up to the neutron. **Open:** whether and when Japan is told what follows; his later career and scenes.

**Voice:** Patient, quietly stubborn, a dissenter another school takes in.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** Inside the wall. In 1920, after Hahn publishes, he argues that silence now hides only Pacifica's head start, a deception of the world in all but name; he loses, resigns, is held to his bond and returns to Tokyo Imperial University, where he keeps the seal even from his own government. His silence is the proof Julian needs that a Japanese scientist can carry it, and it opens the way for Nishina in 1922. Both crowns honour him in 1927. PROPOSED: in the 1890s he proposes a ring of electrons around the core, the Pacifican model that fails; in 1916–1917 he leads the test that proves the light isotope is the one that splits.

**APPROVED — CR-051:** His case of 1920 includes the true signposts left standing to mislead Europe.

people.narrative_profile:
**Status:** Historical person in alternate history (CR-049).

**APPROVED — CR-049:** Born in 1890. The Japanese co-lead of the atomic programme; atomic energy is the emblem of Pacifica's friendship with Japan, and an atomic power station lights Tokyo. **Open:** when he joins, when and how Japan is told, his part in the Tokyo station and scenes.

**APPROVED — CR-050:** He enters the walled college in 1922, after his first European years. From about 1924 his group designs the Tokyo station inside the wall; ground is broken in 1928, the year of Hirohito's enthronement, with Japanese engineers his group has trained, first power comes in 1931 and the station opens on 29 April 1932.
